items.title: Modi-Putin once again share a car ride post talks
items.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin met on Friday on the margins of the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, according to an official readout from the Prime Minister's Office.This was their second meeting this year, following talks in Bishkek on the sidelines of the 26th SCO Summit on August 31, 2026.Putin had arrived in the capital earlier in the day and was welcomed upon arrival by Union Minister of State for External Affairs Kirti Vardhan Singh.The Thirukkural giftDuring the talks, PM Modi gifted Putin a Russian translation of the Thirukkural, the classical Tamil scripture composed by the weaver-saint Thiruvalluvar. "Two thousand years ago, Thiruvalluvar wrote the Thirukkural.It includes the entire gamut of human life. It has been translated into the Russian language. I am confident that the people-to-people contact will increase with the translation of the Thirukkural into Russian, which will play a big role in strengthening our relations," PM Modi told Putin.Also read: What is Thirukkural? 2,500-year-old ancient Tamil text written by poet Thiruvalluvar that PM Modi gifted to Vladimir Putin during BRICS SummitThe Thirukkural consists of 1,330 couplets, each two lines long, structured around three universal values — aram (virtue), porul (wealth and statecraft), and inbam (love). Revered by Tamils as a sacred scripture, it is often referred to as "the Tamil Veda".What the two leaders discussedAccording to the PMO, Modi and Putin reviewed progress in bilateral cooperation across political, economic, defence, energy, space, skill mobility and people-to-people domains. They welcomed Russia's International Industrial Exhibition "INNOPROM India", held for the first time in India from September 9-11, and underscored its importance in expanding trade and industrial ties between the two countries. The two leaders also visited the INNOPROM India exhibition together and interacted with participants.— ANI (@ANI) The leaders also exchanged views on India-Russia engagement in the multilateral sphere, particularly within BRICS under India's Chairship for 2026, and shared perspectives on regional and global issues of mutual interest, including the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region, which have affected maritime trade as well as the safety and security of Indian seafarers. PM Modi reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy remained the way forward in resolving these conflicts, and that India stood ready to assist in peace efforts.The two sides agreed to remain engaged in strengthening the Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership between the two countries further, noting that it continues to register significant growth and has shown resilience amid geopolitical uncertainties. President Putin also invited PM Modi to visit Russia for the 24th India-Russia Annual Summit, an invitation the Prime Minister accepted; the dates for the summit will be finalised through diplomatic channels.The INNOPROM visitINNOPROM, the International Industrial Exhibition, is a global platform bringing together manufacturers and buyers from around the world, offering a venue to showcase technologies, access international markets, and network on B2B opportunities. Its presence in India this year was part of the broader push to deepen India-Russia industrial ties.India's BRICS Chairship this year is guided by the theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability", with development, sustainability and innovation as key focus areas. BRICS has emerged as an important platform for coordination among major emerging economies and for advancing the interests of the Global South in multilateral institutions, with an agenda covering development, finance, technology, trade and people-to-people exchanges.Also read: Elephant, Dragon & Bear: Modi, Xi and Putin may converge at BRICS for a big power playThe grouping currently comprises 11 countries — Brazil, China, Egypt, Ethiopia, India, Indonesia, Iran, Russia, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UAE — which together account for around 49.5% of the global population, 40% of global GDP, and 26% of global trade, according to background information on India's 2026 Chairship. India's Chairship comes amid global economic fragmentation, technological disruption, geopolitical uncertainty, climate change and resource pressures.Friday's bilateral was Modi and Putin's second meeting this year and the latest in a continuing pattern of leader-level engagement between the two countries, including their meeting on the sidelines of the 26th SCO Summit in Bishkek on August 31, 2026. The 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi is expected to bring together leaders and senior representatives from across the grouping over the two-day meeting starting Saturday.(With inputs from ANI)

items.summary:
Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 2026 which got assent of the President of India last month, and is aimed at providing a modern framework for the use of banking records as evidence in line with contemporary banking practices, will come into force from October 1.
The notification dated September 10 appoints October 1, 2026 as the date on which provisions of the Act will come into force, the finance ministry said in a statement on Friday.
The Act adopts a technology-neutral approach by recognising banking records maintained in physical, electronic, digital, virtual, cloud-based and other contemporary forms, it said.
It also provides for simplified and standardised certification of banking records, including through manual, digital or electronic signatures.

items.title: Alembic Pharma clears USFDA inspection at Vadodara bioequivalence facility
items.summary:
Alembic Pharmaceuticals on Friday said the US health regulator has completed an unannounced inspection at its bioequivalence facility in Vadodara, Gujarat, with zero observation.
In a regulatory filing, the company said the United States Food and Drug Administration (USFDA) carried out the onsite bioequivalence inspection from August 31, 2026, to September 10, 2026.
The inspection concluded with no Form 483 observations, it added.
In USFDA parlance, an FDA Form 483 is issued to a firm's management at the conclusion of an inspection when investigators observe conditions that may violate the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and related regulations. No observations under this rule indicate a clean outcome.

items.title: Canada work permit delays rise in August
items.summary: Canada’s processing time for Labour Market Impact Assessments (LMIAs) jumped sharply in August, with employers waiting an average of 156 days for the permanent resident stream, up from 86 days in July. The latest figures from Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), released on September 10, show that processing times increased in most Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP) streams.Permanent resident stream sees biggest riseThe permanent resident stream recorded the biggest increase, with the average wait rising by 70 days in one month. The low-wage stream also saw a notable increase, with processing time going up from 73 days in July to 82 days in August.Also Read: Indians can visit UAE to seek jobs without a local employer or sponsor: What you need to knowFor the high-wage stream, the wait increased from 88 days to 90 days. The agricultural stream rose from 23 days to 25 days. The Global Talent Stream remained unchanged at 10 days. This means it continued to meet ESDC’s 10-day service standard.The Seasonal Agricultural Worker Program was the only stream where processing became faster. Its average wait fell from eight days to six days.What the LMIA wait times meanAn LMIA is generally needed when a Canadian employer wants to hire a temporary foreign worker through the TFWP.The assessment checks whether the employer made efforts to find a Canadian citizen or permanent resident for the job and whether hiring a foreign worker could affect the Canadian labour market.Also Read: Trump’s H-1B crackdown hurts Indian IT, but the industry saw it comingThe processing times published by ESDC show the average number of business days needed to assess an application. They do not include the advertising period that employers must complete before applying. Depending on the stream, this can take between 14 days and eight weeks.Canada is also reducing temporary worker numbersThe increase in LMIA processing times comes as Canada continues to reduce the number of temporary foreign workers it plans to admit.The government has set a target of 60,000 TFWP admissions in 2026, down from 82,000 in 2025.In the first half of 2026, 23,190 temporary foreign workers entered Canada. That was 42.1% lower than the number recorded during the same period in 2025.Low-wage LMIA applications also face restrictions in regions where the unemployment rate is 6% or higher. The federal government updates the list of affected regions every quarter.

items.title: IPO STREET: RENTOMOJO, ARCIL, MANIPAL PAYMENTS & KARAMTARA — DECODED BY MONEYCONTROL RESEARCH
items.summary: India's IPO market is witnessing intense action, with 81 companies having already raised over Rs 83,000 crore by going public so far this year, a number set to grow further with NSE set to launch its much-awaited public issue next week. The week of September 7 to 11 saw frenzied primary market activity, with as many as 12 IPOs launched over the past five days, four of which are still open for subscription. On today's IPO Street, we take stock of these four companies gearing up to begin their listed market journey. In focus is Rentomojo, a well-known furniture and appliance rental solutions company; ARCIL, or Asset Reconstruction Company of India Limited, a financial giant that looks to generate returns by turning around distressed and bad loan assets; Manipal Payments and Identity Solutions, a Manipal Group company that manufactures debit and credit cards, offers secure payment solutions, and also operates in the government ID ecosystem, producing documents like voter cards and driving licenses; and Karamtara Engineering, a niche engineering company manufacturing key products and components for the power transmission and renewable energy sectors. To make sense of these four new listings, Moneycontrol's research team joins the show to break down the issue details, business fundamentals, financials and valuation, and their view on each offering.

Justice Anish Dayal issued notice to the governments on a petition seeking directions to them to complete the statutory process for constitution of the Board in accordance with the Waqf Act of 1995, as amended by the Waqf (Amendment) Act, 2025.

On September 8, Justice Dayal gave four weeks to the Delhi government and Centre to file their replies.

Marcos Jr. — President of the PhilippinesBruno Rodriguez Parrilla — Minister of Foreign Affairs of CubaDr Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala — Director-General of the World Trade OrganizationMaxim Ryzhenkov — Minister of Foreign Affairs of BelarusLe Minh Hung — Prime Minister of VietnamXi Jinping — President of ChinaDr Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani — Minister of Foreign Affairs of BahrainKassym-Jomart Tokayev — President of KazakhstanPrince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud — Minister of Foreign Affairs of Saudi ArabiaAlso read: Bilats, brush-bys, pull-asides: The secret art of summitry at BRICSModi Putin meetLater in the day PM Modi is set to hold a bilateral meeting with Putin ahead of the two-day summit that gets underway on Saturday.The much-awaited discussions are expected to focus on strategic trade resilience, cross-border payment mechanisms, energy security, and conflict-resolution pathways regarding ongoing geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe and West Asia.According to a statement issued by the Kremlin, the Russian president will address the plenary session of the annual BRICS Business Forum on September 11, a platform that traditionally precedes the leaders' summit and brings together business representatives from BRICS countries.On Saturday, PM Modi will participate in the BRICS Summit where several world leaders including Chinese President Xi Jinping will be present.What is BRICS?BRICS has emerged as a key international platform for coordinating economic policy among major emerging economies. items.title: Russian Prez Vladimir Putin arrives in New Delhi to attend Brics summit

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday began a three-day visit to India to participate in the BRICS summit and meet Prime Minister Narendra Modi to expand bilateral trade, investment and energy cooperation.
Putin is accompanied by a high-level delegation.
It will be his first in-person participation at a BRICS summit outside Russia since the war in Ukraine began in February 2022.
The two-day BRICS summit hosted by India starting Saturday is expected to focus on boosting collective resilience in food, energy, health, disaster reduction and critical supply chains with New Delhi positioning the bloc as an effective anchor to navigate a fragmented geopolitical environment.
The summit in New Delhi is taking place against the backdrop of a global economy facing the adverse impacts of the Russia-Ukraine war, the West Asia crisis, especially the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, and the Trump administration's trade and tariff policies.

items.title: ET 40 Under 40: Meet India's 40 young leaders
items.summary: The Economic Times 40 under Forty returns for its 12th edition with a cohort that reflects just how much the idea of leadership has changed over the years. The 40 honorees for 2026 come from a wide range of fields—business, finance and professional services to technology, law, social impact, art, culture and sports—and offer a broader view of the people shaping the country’s next chapter.The diversity of the cohort is striking, highlighting the many paths young professionals are taking toward success and leadership. Some are building businesses from the ground up while others are steering family enterprises into new territories. There are investors deploying capital, professionals leading organisations through change, innovators creating new products and ideas, and individuals influencing India’s legal, social and cultural landscape.Financial services, venture capital and private equity have the highest representation this year, accounting for 17.5% of the list, with seven honorees, while those from professional services (5) account for 12.5%. Owner professionals; consumer and luxury; technology, media, telecom and legal services contribute four (10%) honorees each. Three achievers (7.5%) from the industrial sector and another two (5%) from the social sector add to the eclectic mix. Two (5%) global Indians feature on the list as well, underscoring the reach of the country's talent across geographies.134029366The inclusion of five people (12.5%) from art, culture and sports is particularly significant. It recognises that some of India’s most influential voices are building their impact through creativity, cultural influence, grit, determination and on-ground performance. Women make up 11 of this year’s 40 honorees, representing 27.5% of the cohort, marking their highest representation in the list since the seventh edition.134029416Over the years, The Economic Times 40 under Forty has evolved into an important marker of young talent across India’s changing economy. The class of 2026 adds another 40 names to an alumni base that numbers 440, many of whom have gone on to shape businesses and institutions.134029559METHODOLOGYThe Economic Times has compiled its list of India’s top 40 leaders under forty — a celebration of the country’s most dynamic and promising talent — for the 12th year. The process began with the formation of a distinguished jury tasked with identifying India’s next generation of leaders.134029598Nominations were invited through multiple channels: self and corporate nominations; recommendations from the 440-strong ET 40 Under Forty alumni network; and inputs from leading executive search firms such as Accord and EMA Partners, among others, as well as the ET Leadership team. Together, these efforts yielded an extensive pool of over 650 nominations.134029628The preliminary list featured a diverse mix of professionals, entrepreneurs and owner-promoters across industries. A rigorous multi-stage evaluation followed. Team ET conducted the first round of screening, shortlisting 250 profiles based on scale, impact, innovation and value creation. Further detailed assessments, incorporating insights from ET’s senior editorial and leadership teams, along with perspectives from industry experts, narrowed this down to 113 finalists.134029683The jury evaluated these 113 nominees for impact, innovation, integrity, leadership, and potential for future contributions, ultimately selecting the final list of 40.134029715The eligibility threshold for the 2026 list was March 31, 2026 — candidates should not have turned 41 as of that date.134029836134029864134029898134029931134029968134029996134030023134030055134030090

IAMAI seeks GST cut for app-based rides
items.summary: New Delhi: The app-based mobility industry has pitched for exemption from the 5% goods and services tax (GST), arguing that the levy is being imposed on platforms that often do not collect fares from passengers.In a representation to the government and the Goods and Services Tax Council, the Internet and Mobile Association of India (IAMAI) said the current tax structure does not reflect how several ride-hailing platforms actually operate.On these platforms, a driver collects the fare directly from the passenger and the app acts primarily as a technology platform connecting the two, it said. Yet, the industry body said the platform is required to account for the 5% GST on the value of the ride.The IAMAI said this creates an unfair tax burden that ultimately gets passed on to drivers or passengers.The association made a case for excluding such technology-based platforms from the provision under Section 9(5) of the CGST Act that shifts the GST responsibility for passenger transport services to the digital platform.The industry body also flagged conflicting rulings by state tax authorities on whether such platforms fall under the provision, saying the lack of clarity has left the sector facing prolonged uncertainty.

items.title: US wholesale inventories surge in July
items.summary: U.S. wholesale inventories surged in ​July, the government ​confirmed on Thursday, potentially positioning inventories ​to contribute to economic growth in the third quarter.Stocks at wholesalers jumped by an unrevised 1.3%, ‌the Commerce ⁠Department's Census ⁠Bureau said. Inventories, a key part of gross ​domestic product, increased 0.4% in July. They rose 5.7% ​on a year-over-year basis in July.Businesses are replenishing inventories, which have been drawn ​down for five straight ⁠quarters amid ‌robust domestic demand. Inventories subtracted 0.72 ​percentage ​point from gross domestic product growth ⁠in the second quarter. The economy ​grew at a 1.5% annualized rate ​last quarter.Growth estimates for the July-September quarter are currently running well above a 2% pace.The surge in wholesale inventories in July was driven by durable goods, ‌which increased 1.1%. Stocks of nondurable goods shot up 1.6%, with ​petroleum inventories ​increasing 6.5%.Sales ⁠at wholesalers rebounded 0.8% in July after dropping 2.9% in June. At July's sales pace ​it would take 1.20 months to clear shelves, up from 1.19 months in June. The inventories/sales ratio was at 1.28 months in July 2025.

Pakistan on Thursday termed the trilateral defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye as a "defensive alliance" to ensure regional security primarily through deterrence and ruled out any quick expansion of the pact.
Pakistan, Turkiye and Saudi Arabia signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement in Makkah on August 7. The pact establishes a framework for collective deterrence and stipulates that an armed attack against any one of the three countries would be regarded as an attack against all three.
The trilateral agreement was primarily a "defensive alliance to ensure regional security primarily through deterrence," Foreign Office spokesperson Sajjad Haider Khan said at the weekly press briefing.
His remarks came two days after Defence Minister Khawaja Asif on Tuesday said that an unprovoked aggression against any member state, or a spillover of the Yemen conflict into Saudi Arabia, could activate the collective-defence provisions of the agreement.

items.title: US unemployment claims dip to 206,000
items.summary: Slightly fewer Americans filed for unemployment claims last week as jobless claims remain at historically low levels and layoffs are still relatively rare.Filings for benefits dipped to 206,000 last week from a revised 207,000 the week before, the Labor Department reported Thursday. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, also fell modestly to 206,000.Claims for jobless benefits are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed. For the past year, claims have mostly stayed within a historically low range of 200,000 to 230,000 a week.The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher gasoline prices that have squeezed businesses and consumers since the fighting with Iran began Feb. 28.Layoffs are low. Businesses, remembering the labor shortages that followed the end of pandemic lockdowns, are reluctant to let go of staff. They're hiring - but modestly by the standards of recent years.So far this year, employers - companies, government agencies and nonprofits - have been adding an average 80,000 jobs a month, including a surprising 162,000 in August. That is an improvement on a dismal 2025 when monthly job creation averaged less than 10,000 as high interest rates and President Donald Trump's erratic trade policies discouraged hiring.But it remains well below the 166,000 monthly jobs created, on average, in 2023 and 2024, let alone the 491,000 a month recorded during the 2021-2022 hiring boom that followed COVID-19 lockdowns.

items.title: New India industrial revolution takes shape
items.summary: New Delhi: India is entering a new phase of industrialisation as rising domestic demand and government support draw private capital into emerging sectors including space, semiconductors, data centres, electronics and solar manufacturing, brokerage Jefferies said in a report.The government has backed the push through measures including opening the space sector to private companies, tax incentives for data centres, large production-linked schemes for semiconductors, electronics and solar, localisation requirements and purchases of GPUs.The resulting investment cycle is creating opportunities not only in end-product manufacturing but also across domestic supply chains, components, infrastructure and engineering services, it said.Also read | Bilats, brush-bys, pull-asides: The secret art of summitry at BRICSOn the space sector, Jefferies said India is among a handful of spacefaring nations with globally competitive capabilities. The government opened the sector to private participation in 2020 and is targeting an almost five-fold expansion of the space economy between 2023 and 2030, to about USD 40 billion-USD 45 billion.Indian startups are increasingly moving from early-stage innovation toward commercial execution. Skyroot is targeting an orbital launch in July, while Pixxel is developing high-resolution earth-observation satellites. Agnikul is working on 3D-printed rocket engines and Digantara is developing satellite-based space-surveillance capabilities.The shift is broadening private-sector participation beyond satellite services into launch vehicles, propulsion, earth observation and space situational awareness.The brokerage said India's semiconductor ambitions are moving from policy planning toward execution, with about USD 20 billion of investments announced or underway, including a chip fabrication plant under construction and several outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) projects moving toward production.A new incentive plan worth about USD 13 billion is expected to further expand the ecosystem and increase domestic value addition, including in chip design.Also read | 7 cases dropped: HDFC scores big win in BahrainSupply-chain depth, availability of skilled talent and competition from established semiconductor hubs remain challenges. But the investment pipeline is laying the foundations for a domestic semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem.On the data-centre industry, it said India has emerged as a strategic digital-infrastructure segment, with co-location capacity rising five-fold over the past five years to about 2 gigawatts.Cloud adoption, digitisation and data-localisation requirements are driving demand. Capacity could expand another five-fold to about 10 GW over the next five years, supported by favourable cost economics, policy measures and rising demand from hyperscalers.That expansion could represent about USD 9 billion in revenue for data-centre operators and roughly USD 45 billion of investment across power, cooling, construction and network infrastructure, according to the report.Jefferies said India's electronics industry is entering a new phase, with policymakers and manufacturers focusing increasingly on domestic value addition and component production.Electronics exports have risen sharply, while schemes including the Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS) and Mobile 2.0 are intended to deepen backward integration and reduce dependence on imports.The report forecasts that ECMS could cover about 50 per cent of the bill of materials for mobile components over the next six years, compared with less than 20 per cent currently.Printed circuit boards, including high-density interconnect and multi-layer boards, are a particular focus. The segment has an estimated USD 5 billion total addressable market, with 85-90 per cent of demand currently met through imports.The brokerage said India has emerged as the world's second-largest solar photovoltaic manufacturer, with about 35 GW of solar-cell capacity operational and another 100 GW under construction.Policy measures including the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM), domestic-content requirements and production-linked incentives are encouraging greater integration across the solar manufacturing chain, including cells, wafers and ingots.The report expects about 90 per cent of the solar manufacturing value chain to be localised by 2030.India is also positioned to benefit from a global supply-demand imbalance in aerospace, leveraging relatively competitive manufacturing costs and its engineering talent pool, it said, adding that Boeing and Airbus already source an estimated USD 1.4-1.6 billion annually from India, while domestic companies including Aequs, Azad, BHFC, DYTC, RW, MOTHERSO and SANSERA are supplying global original-equipment manufacturers and Tier-1 suppliers and expanding their aerospace businesses.The opportunity extends beyond outsourcing into higher-value manufacturing and engineering as global aerospace companies diversify supply chains.The common thread across these industries is a push to move India higher up global supply chains. Government incentives are being combined with a large domestic market, rising digitisation, strategic localisation and growing demand for manufacturing and infrastructure.Space and semiconductors are relatively new areas of private-sector participation, while electronics and solar are moving from import dependence and assembly toward greater domestic value addition. Data centres are emerging as a major infrastructure build-out, and aerospace offers an avenue for Indian manufacturers to capture a larger share of global production.Together, these sectors point to a broader industrial strategy: use India's domestic demand and policy support to build local capabilities, attract private investment and position Indian companies deeper inside global technology and manufacturing supply chains.

items.title: Asian Games: Asmita sharpens ground game to counter formidable Japan

Inspired by the Japanese but equally wary of the challenge they will pose, India's Commonwealth Games gold-winning judoka Asmita Dey says she is trying to sharpen her holds, pins and submission techniques to present a strong challenge at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya.
Dey said she has spent considerable time trying to ace the three aspects of ground fighting as the Asian Games will be a significantly tougher test than the CWG in Glasgow, where she became the first Indian judoka to win a gold.
"The Asian Games, as compared to the Commonwealth Games, will be very tough for me because at the Asian Games we have some of the world's best from rankings 7-14 competing there," the 23-year-old Dey told PTI Videos as she looked forward to her maiden appearance at the Asian Games beginning September 19.
"Our master in Judo is Japan, so Japanese judokas are also there, so it is tough for me. I need to work on my Ne-Waza because if I am in the final, my opponent will most likely be Japanese.

items.title: Champions League: Odegaard seals Arsenal win at Napoli with late strike
items.summary:
Arsenal's perfect start to the season continued in the Champions League thanks to Martin degaard's sudden rush of goals.
degaard struck with a powerful left-foot shot in the 75th minute to secure a 1-0 win at Napoli that should have been more decisive.

items.title: Kant's 3-step formula for India's BRICS move
items.summary: India must ensure that the language of the BRICS summit document is progressive and forward-looking, Amitabh Kant, former India G20 Sherpa and former chief executive officer of NITI Aayog, highlighted ahead of the bloc's summit beginning September 11."It is important that we are able to resolve the differences despite the conflict in West Asia. When you have Iran, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, it is highly complex. But India must play a key role in getting the right minimum language to be able to resolve this," Kant said. He added that, apart from the BRICS summit, there would be significant bilateral engagement.Also read: China's Xi Jinping to visit India for first time in seven years as New Delhi hosts BRICS Summit"The Prime Minister will be meeting Putin and Xi Jinping, and the China-India play on issues of development, trade and technology is critical," Kant said at the India Today BRICS Roundtable.Kant said he expected further movement in India-China relations, which had been progressing smoothly before tensions led India to introduce Press Note 3. He also referred to changes in the foreign direct investment framework, saying that beneficial ownership had now been defined under Press Note 3, allowing up to 10% investment by Chinese entities under specified conditions."But we need a movement forward. We need to advance this forward," Kant said.Kant's three step formula:India should push for a progressive, forward-looking BRICS summit document and help bridge differences over West Asia.Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s meetings with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping could drive significant bilateral engagement alongside the summit.India should push for further movement in ties with China, particularly on development, trade and technology.Former NITI Aayog chief said India’s foreign policy has been shaped by a strategy of being “multi-aligned”, allowing it to deepen economic partnerships across competing geopolitical blocs while pursuing its growth ambitions.“To achieve our ambition of economic growth, we have done multiple FTAs. But we also have to work with Russia and China,” Kant said, arguing that India cannot afford to view its economic and strategic relationships through the lens of a single alliance.Also read: BRICS Summit 2026: Stage set at Bharat Mandapam as PM Modi hosts expanded global powerhouseEnergy security will remain a key challenge, he said, particularly as India pursues its ambition of becoming a developed economy. India will continue to require fossil fuel imports for the foreseeable future, with energy purchases adding pressure on the rupee and affecting the broader economy.Kant also flagged the strategic implications of developments in West Asia, saying that if the US were to succeed in controlling Iranian crude, it could potentially gain majority influence over a significant share of the world's fossil fuel resources.India will therefore need to navigate its relationships with major powers carefully, including the US and China, while safeguarding its energy and economic interests, he said.On China, Kant said Beijing's economic model remains heavily focused on exports rather than imports, while its domestic market continues to be marked by non-tariff barriers.India should use bilateral discussions with China to press for the transfer of clean-energy technologies to other BRICS partners, Kant said. He argued that China's dominance over critical clean-energy technologies had become a strategic concern, with Beijing increasingly “weaponising” its technological capabilities.“We do a very substantial amount of imports from China. It's very important to understand that China is weaponising all its new technologies,” Kant said.He highlighted this should also be a key issue during PM Modi's bilateral engagement with Chinese President Xi Jinping. India, he said, must understand the implications of China's control over clean-energy supply chains, particularly technologies such as batteries, where concentrated market power can influence prices.Kant said India must simultaneously strengthen its own technological capabilities. He pointed to the opening up of key sectors such as geospatial services, drones and space, along with India's push into cutting-edge technologies including semiconductors, as two major developments.These initiatives could give India “quantum growth”, he said.As India gears up to host BRICS, Kant said the country should focus its agenda on trade, investment, development and climate issues. BRICS nations account for a significant share of global trade, and greater cooperation could benefit economies across the Global South, he added.A key lesson from India's G20 presidency, according to Kant, is the importance of building consensus through multilateral negotiations. Achieving consensus should be the hallmark of India's BRICS presidency as well, he said, particularly given the expansion of the grouping and the differing interests of its members.At the same time, Kant stressed the importance of India's relationship with the US.“No country has made wealth without working with the US,” he said, arguing that India must act as a “mature, seasoned player” capable of steering through increasingly turbulent geopolitical conditions.India's ability to build consensus among countries with competing strategic and economic interests could itself become a major achievement during its BRICS presidency, he said.Beyond geopolitical conflicts and disruptions to global supply chains, Kant said BRICS must also confront the rapid emergence of artificial intelligence as one of the biggest drivers of global change.“While there are conflicts that break down the supply chain, there's also the emergence of artificial intelligence as a very key driver for global growth and prosperity,” he said.The growing global competition around AI also makes it essential to establish frameworks for its responsible use, Kant added.

"Chunni Lal Bhagat ji is no longer with us. We are deeply saddened by his demise,  Mohinder Bhagat, who is the Horticulture minister in the AAP government, said.

Lal was a cabinet minister in the erstwhile SAD-BJP government in 2012. He held the portfolios of Local Government and Medical Education and Research in the then Parkash Singh Badal government.

items.title: Huawei racketeering trial begins in US as prosecutors allege theft, spying
items.summary:
A racketeering conspiracy trial against Huawei Technologies began in New York on Wednesday with federal prosecutors accusing the Chinese tech company of a litany of crimes, including stealing technology from American companies, abusing the US financial system and helping Iran snoop on its citizens.
Huawei is the world's biggest supplier of gear for wireless telecom networks, but it is banned from selling equipment to US carriers over fears it poses a security risk. It has also been blacklisted by other Western allies, including Canada and Britain.
Taylor Stout, a Department of Justice attorney, opened the government's case by telling the Brooklyn jury that Huawei committed multiple crimes over two decades.
Defence attorney Brian Heberlig dismissed the accusations, though, saying prosecutors were basing their case on a smattering of anecdotes and some bad behaviour by a few of Huawei's roughly 200,000 employees in 170 countries to cast the company and three of its subsidiaries as a .

Apple has also added new professional camera controls, improved video capabilities and enhanced AI-powered photography tools.iPhone 18 Pro launched at $ 1,119 The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are powered by the new A20 Pro chip, built around a redesigned architecture focused on performance and efficiency. The chip features a six-core CPU with new performance and efficiency cores, with CPU performance up to 20% faster than the previous generation. The GPU has also received a major upgrade, with a seven-core design delivering significant gains in graphics performance and AI-powered image generation.The new neural engine is specifically designed for on-device AI workloads, with a 32-core design and support for advanced 8-bit floating-point operations. Together, the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine improvements make the A20 Pro significantly more capable of running demanding Apple Intelligence features directly on the iPhone. Apple has also increased memory bandwidth by 50%, helping the device handle larger AI models and demanding applications more efficiently.More powerful Apple Intelligence and SiriThe new Pro models bring deeper Apple Intelligence capabilities, including access to Apple's latest Foundation models and more powerful on-device AI models. Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro can run its most advanced on-device models yet, enabling features such as enhanced image generation, smarter photo editing and more capable Siri interactions.Siri is also getting a major upgrade. Users can interact with Siri more naturally, continue conversations across Apple devices and use the assistant to take actions across supported apps. Siri can understand information displayed through the camera and help users act on what they see. Apple Intelligence also brings more personalised capabilities, including creating automations through natural-language instructions, finding information across apps and generating images through Image Playground.Apple says the new capabilities will work across more than 3,000 apps, allowing developers to integrate Apple's AI features into everyday workflows.New 48MP camera with variable apertureOne of the biggest upgrades comes to the camera system. The iPhone 18 Pro introduces a new 48MP Fusion main camera with variable aperture, giving users more control over how much light enters the camera and how much of the scene remains in focus.The variable-aperture system can automatically adjust depending on the scene, while also allowing users to manually control the aperture for greater creative flexibility. A wider aperture can create a shallower depth of field, while a narrower aperture can keep more of the scene in focus. Apple has also introduced new Pro controls, allowing users to manually adjust settings such as white balance, exposure, histogram and shutter speed.For video creators, the iPhone 18 Pro adds more advanced controls and improved cinematic capabilities. Users can adjust shutter speed for motion blur, while AI-powered smart focus tracking can maintain focus on moving subjects. The new system also supports improved Dolby Vision HDR video and enhanced audio recording capabilities.New tools for photographersApple is also expanding its computational photography capabilities. Photographic Styles now offer additional control over texture and grain, allowing users to create more distinctive looks while retaining control over colour and skin tones. The iPhone 18 Pro also introduces a new approach to preserving image authenticity. Apple says captured images can retain additional information that can be used to verify what was actually recorded by the camera.Together with the new variable-aperture camera and Pro controls, Apple says the system is designed to offer greater flexibility for both everyday photography and professional workflows.Improved thermal managementApple has redesigned the thermal architecture of the iPhone 18 Pro to help sustain the higher performance of the A20 Pro chip. The new thermal system features a next-generation vapour chamber with three times the surface area of the system used in the iPhone 17 Pro. Apple has also introduced new thermal materials, including a nano-twin copper material designed to move heat away from the display more effectively. The company says the redesigned thermal system can deliver up to a 40% improvement in sustained performance compared with the previous-generation Pro model.Longest battery life ever on an iPhoneBattery life is another major focus of the new Pro models. The iPhone 18 Pro offers up to 36 hours of video playback, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max delivers up to 45 hours, giving the Max model the longest battery life ever offered on an iPhone. Apple has also improved charging, with the iPhone 18 Pro capable of reaching 50% charge in around 15 minutes under supported conditions.More connectivity and iOS 27 featuresThe iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max also benefit from new software and connectivity features in iOS 27. Apple says AirDrop transfers are up to 80% faster, while connectivity has been improved with smarter transitions between Wi-Fi networks. A new feature called iPhone Handoff allows a single phone number to be used across two iPhones, with the number becoming active on whichever iPhone the user picks up. The Pro models also feature an upgraded Dynamic Island, while iOS 27 brings further customisation and improvements across apps including Mail and other system experiences.iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max price and availabilityThe iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299 in the US. Pre-orders for both models begin September 12, with availability starting September 18. With the A20 Pro chip, deeper on-device Apple Intelligence, a new variable-aperture 48MP camera, improved thermal architecture and the longest battery life ever on an iPhone, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max represent Apple's biggest Pro upgrade across performance, photography and AI.

items.title: Microsoft is funding a bet on mud
items.summary: Warblers and sparrows call across the treetops at sunrise. Deer browse the shrubs. Black bears turn over roots for insects. Above ground, this stretch of North Carolina's Inner Banks looks like farmland, cotton and soybeans and corn running to the horizon.The reason scientists and investors have converged on this 60-square-kilometre tract is underneath it: dense, spongy peat, up to five metres deep, the Associated Press reported.Decades ago, an abandoned farming venture cut 80 kilometres of ditches through the site and drained the water out of soil that had taken thousands of years to accumulate. That left it exposed to drought and fire, altered the habitat, and turned a carbon store into a carbon source. The site now emits about 130,000 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year."Our goal is for perpetuity to conserve these lands so they can't become oil and gas fields, so they're not mined for phosphorus or turned into parking lots and shopping centers," Tripp Wall, chief executive of the Colorado-based company Pantheon Regeneration, told AP. He described peatlands as underappreciated systems that had been climatologically resilient for 10,000 to 15,000 years "until we screwed them up."Why peat matters more than forestPeatlands cover roughly 3% of the planet's land surface. They hold close to a third of all soil carbon, which is about twice as much as the biomass of every forest on Earth combined, according to the UN Environment Programme.The mechanism is simple. When peat is waterlogged, decomposing plant matter sits in an oxygen-starved environment and the gases stay trapped, while the vegetation on the surface keeps pulling carbon dioxide out of the air. Drain it and the process reverses.That reversal is now a significant emissions source in its own right. UNEP's Global Peatlands Assessment put emissions from drained and degraded peatlands at around 4% of annual human-caused greenhouse gas emissions, from an area equal to roughly 0.4% of the world's land surface. The AP report cites a higher current figure of about 6% of the annual global total.Two-thirds of temperate peatlands, mostly in Europe and the United States, have been dewatered. About 45% of tropical peatlands have been similarly disturbed. Boreal peatlands in Canada and Russia remain roughly 90% intact but face thawing permafrost, intensifying fires and pressure from mining and critical minerals exploration.Only 17% of the world's peatlands sit inside a protected area, according to a study published in Conservation Letters, the journal of the Society for Conservation Biology, in February 2025. For comparison, protected areas cover 38% of tropical forests, 42% of mangroves and 50% of saltmarshes."This is the black gold"Neal Flanagan pushes a metal tube down through roots and buried logs until it sinks about a metre, then pulls out a core packed with black soil. Near the top it is dry, full of dead fibres from wood fern and blueberry. The middle is crumbly and odourless, flecked with charcoal from old fires. The saturated bottom is half carbon and has the consistency of axle grease."This is the black gold," said Duke University ecologist Curtis Richardson, letting ancient peat ooze from his fist. Its "magnitude and importance cannot be underestimated," he told AP.The North Carolina variety, called Pocosin peat, formed from coastal pine forests and evergreen shrubs decaying over millennia. Domed peatlands of this type exist only along the Eastern Seaboard. In North Carolina alone, 17,700 kilometres of canals drain peatlands into coastal estuaries, Richardson said.Fires that burn underground for monthsSaturated peat is close to fireproof. Only surface vegetation and a few inches of peat burn, releasing nutrients and regenerating seed banks.Dry peat is a different proposition. Fire moves underground and can smoulder for weeks or months, drying out and consuming even the saturated layers below.A 2008 fire that started during a drought burned above ground for three months and smouldered underground for four more, damaging over a quarter of the neighbouring Pocosin Lakes National Wildlife Refuge and dropping the ground level by several feet in places, refuge manager Sarah Toner said. Where water-level restoration had already begun, the fire burned less deeply.A more recent fire burned about 800 hectares nearby four years ago, lowering the ground by half a metre in places. The North Carolina Forest Service and other agencies put it out in roughly three weeks by pumping water from nearby lakes."We'll lose 5, 6 feet of peat in a matter of weeks, which equates to millions of tons of carbon loss, ancient carbon loss that we simply can't ever get back in human lifetimes," Richardson said.That risk is why Pantheon is prioritising drained sites over intact ones. "There's this urgency to start with what's degraded now," Wall said, "before it goes away."The business modelThe restoration itself is not novel. Pantheon plans to block the ditches to raise the water table, then remove invasive species and replant native grasses and flowers, an approach modelled on projects run by nonprofits and government agencies, including at the adjacent 453-square-kilometre Pocosin Lakes refuge, one of the largest peatland restorations in the United States. That refuge supports red wolves, yellow pitcher plants and Atlantic white cedar, and has become a stopover for migrating tundra swans.What is different is how Pantheon intends to pay for it. The company plans to sell carbon credits to technology companies and other corporations offsetting their own emissions, then use the proceeds to restore and permanently conserve about 4,047 square kilometres of peatland from Virginia to northern Florida over the next decade. Microsoft is among the investors providing initial capital for land acquisition, Wall said. Each credit represents one tonne.Carbon credits carry a reputational problem. Over the years, some programmes have been found to overstate how much carbon they captured, and others were outright fraudulent.Pantheon says its credits will be scientifically verified, drawing on Richardson's decades of data on carbon loss at the site, continuous groundwater monitoring, a tower measuring gas absorbed and released, computer modelling and core sampling, with results checked by an outside third party.What comes backSteve Apfelbaum, a plant and animal ecologist running breeding and migratory bird surveys at the site, stops his SUV on a rutted lane to listen. He picks out prairie warblers, a species in decline."We heard hundreds of them today," he said. "What that tells me is that this ecosystem is really important" for their migration. He also hears Nashville warblers, which call from treetops but nest in cavities in the peat.Native reptiles, plants, fish and insects should follow, said Vladimir Roosevelt, Pantheon's operations director. The company released a pair of red wolves two years ago that have since had pups.All of it, Apfelbaum said, depends on getting the water back into the ground first, a solution he argued gets less attention than tree planting."We've all been bear-hugged and distracted by trees," he said, "when it's really soil and peat that hold the most carbon."(With inputs from AP)

Americares lands its biggest gift ever
items.summary: A Connecticut family that will not be identified has given $50 million to the American aid group Americares, the largest single donation in the organisation's 47-year history, the Associated Press reported on Wednesday.The gift lands at an unusual moment. Most global health organisations have spent the past year and a half contracting. Americares is now planning to expand."They definitely understood the moment and wanted to do more to respond to that," Christine Squires, the president and chief executive of Americares, told AP of the donor. The family has been associated with the organisation for three decades and is, in her words, very savvy about global health.Also read: MacKenzie Scott's $100 million donation helped wipe out $40 billion in medical debt—here’s how Jeff Bezos’ ex-wife's strategy worksHalf the money will go toward the group's target of helping 100 million people access quality healthcare by 2030, largely by supplying medicines and equipment to its network of more than 4,000 health centres. The focus will be on under-funded countries in sub-Saharan Africa, the Middle East, North Africa, Asia and Latin America. Americares also plans to increase support for health centres inside the United States, in states where it expects a rise in the number of residents without insurance. The other half goes into the endowment.What was lostAmericares drew roughly 10% of its funding from the US government before the cuts, Squires told AP. The shortfall showed up as cancelled work.A maternal care project in Tanzania lost its support last year. Medical clinics in Colombia serving Venezuelan migrants stayed open for several months on private money before closing. A planned five-year collaboration to build a more resilient medical supply chain across Gaza was scrapped entirely.The organisation now funds itself entirely through individual donors, corporations and private foundations, which Squires said matters as it responds to more than 20 active emergencies, among them the Nepal floods and the Ebola outbreak in Congo.Founded in 1979 and headquartered in Stamford, Connecticut, Americares says it has delivered more than $17 billion in humanitarian aid across 164 countries.The bigger holeThe gift is the latest in a series of private interventions since the Trump administration dismantled the US Agency for International Development in early 2025. The scale of what was withdrawn makes the arithmetic difficult. US foreign aid totalled about $64 billion in 2023, the most recent year with comprehensive figures.Private money has moved, though unevenly. British hedge fund manager Chris Hohn stepped in to keep production running at MANA Nutrition, one of two American manufacturers of the therapeutic peanut paste used to treat severe child malnutrition, after US stop-work orders halted their lines. Hohn had already given the organisation more than $250 million before the crisis.A group of former USAID staff, working outside office hours or after being fired, assembled a list of 80 high-impact programmes and took it to private donors. Their effort, Project Resource Optimization, mobilised more than $110 million in grants, with other emergency funds raising at least $15 million more, taking the total past $125 million within eight months.In March 2025, Jacklyn and Miguel Bezos, the parents of Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, committed up to $500 million to UNICEF's Child Nutrition Fund, structured as a one-to-one match designed to draw in other donors. It was, by UNICEF's own account, the largest investment the agency had ever received from a family. The Gates Foundation, separately, narrowed its priorities.Susan Appe, an associate professor of public administration and policy at the University at Albany who researches how nonprofits handle shifting donor-country priorities, told AP that global health has drawn most of the large donors' attention, which she called reasonable given that lives are at stake. But she said the philanthropic response overall has been slower than researchers in her field expected."I think that a lot of philanthropy scholars like myself have been a bit disappointed with the lag of response," she told AP. "It's kind of, to some degree, business as usual."Nobody involved argues that private giving can substitute for what was cut. A study published in The Lancet in June 2025, analysing data from 133 countries, estimated that USAID-supported programmes had prevented more than 91 million deaths between 2001 and 2021, and projected that sustained cuts could result in over 14 million additional deaths by 2030, including more than 4.5 million children under five. The authors described the projection as a model output with a wide uncertainty range.Also read: Bill Gates never studied at University of Washington, but it paid him $500 as a teen; 5 decades later, Microsoft co-founder is giving it $540 millionThe Trump administration has defended the closure. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in July 2025 that the agency had little to show for itself since the end of the Cold War, and that the State Department would prioritise trade and investment over aid, negotiating directly with countries rather than through nonprofits and contractors.Squires said she hopes the anonymous gift prompts others. A donation of that size signals that people still trust both her organisation and the humanitarian sector, she told AP."It's not only up to individuals," she said. "However, individuals who have the means, who have the passion and can invest like this, will help to bring others along."(With inputs from AP)

"We feel proud that 49 per cent of all real-time payments in the world are happening through India, and it's great. But I hope that other parts of the world capture a lot of the growth.

items.title: Nearly 49% Indian students eye overseas education for better jobs: Report
items.summary:
Students in India are becoming more outcome-focused, as nearly half of aspirants cite better job opportunities as their primary reason for studying abroad, a report said on Wednesday.
According to skilling and workforce development company upGrad's Transnational Education (TNE) Report 2026, around 49 per cent of Indian aspirants revealed better job opportunities as the primary reason for studying abroad, compared to other factors like quality of education, permanent residency or lifestyle aspirations.
Students in India are significantly becoming more result-oriented and are evaluating destinations based on ROI (Return on Investment), employment opportunities and long-term career outcomes over institutional prominence, the report said.
The upGrad report is based on insights from 53,800 counselled aspirants between January 2025 and June 2026.

items.title: Nepal flood death toll climbs to 1,365 as rescue efforts continue
items.summary:
The death toll from the devastating flash floods in Nepal climbed to 1,365 on Wednesday as more bodies were recovered from the affected areas, authorities said.
Rescue teams continued to search for 5,326 people, including at least 589 foreign nationals, who remain missing, according to a Nepal Police news bulletin.
Rescue teams recovered 363 bodies from Chitwan district, 226 from Nawalparasi East, 222 from Nawalparasi West, and 197 from Nuwakot.
Similarly, 174 bodies were recovered from Rasuwa district, 75 from Gorkha, 70 from Dhading and 38 from Tanahu.
So far, 102 bodies have been handed over to the family members after completing the identification process, police said.
Security personnel have safely kept 1,147 unidentified bodies underground in accordance with all prescribed protocols, including the collection of DNA samples to facilitate their identification.

items.title: 'Unacceptable': India condemns Houthi attacks on Saudi oil installations

India on Wednesday condemned the latest wave of attacks carried out by Houthi militants on oil installations in Saudi Arabia, and said the strikes undermined regional security.
The Iran-backed Houthi militant group targeted Saudi oil facilities and some other civilian infrastructure on Tuesday, triggering widespread apprehensions about further escalation in the West Asia conflict.
India condemned the attacks on Saudi sovereign territory, especially the targeting of civilian and economic facilities, External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said.
He added that such attacks that undermined regional security and stability and threatened freedom of navigation in the Bab-el-Mandeb were "unacceptable".
Jaiswal was responding to a media query.
The attacks on Saudi oil facilities came amid the US ramping up its economic sanctions against Iran.
The Houthis have been majorly operating from Yemen.

items.title: UK chaos: Flights resume but delays ahead
items.summary: Flights resumed at major UK airports on Wednesday after an air traffic control system failure cancelled more than 1,000 flights and caused delays across Britain. Heathrow and Gatwick warned that disruption could continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew.Britain’s National Air Traffic Services (NATS) said it had resolved the problem in its flight processing system on Tuesday evening. However, delays continued across 15 UK airports and beyond as airlines and airports worked to clear a backlog of flights.Heathrow resumed departures but suspended arrivals for the rest of Tuesday night. The airport said flights were operating today, but warned that some disruption may continue.Gatwick also said its operations would take time to return to normal.“We still anticipate that it will take time for our operations to fully return to normal,” the airport said.Passengers were left stranded on aircraft, at terminals and at baggage collection areas during the disruption.British Airways cancelled or diverted more than 100 flights. The airline said aircraft and crew had ended up in different locations, affecting its operations.“The severity of the issue means there will be a significant knock-on impact,” a British Airways spokesperson said. “This incident was entirely out of our control and incredibly frustrating for our customers and colleagues, with aircraft and crews ending up out of place.”Passengers on a British Airways flight scheduled to fly from Heathrow to Baltimore spent four hours on the ground before leaving the aircraft. Cabin crew served pasta and chicken curry during the delay, while some passengers watched films or walked through the aisles.Passengers later reported confusion at the baggage claim area and said they were told to file claims for their bags.At Gatwick, Josie Donoghue spent three hours on a plane before her Ryanair flight to Ireland was cancelled.“Getting through that airport was like trying to get out of Alcatraz,” she said, referring to the former island prison in San Francisco Bay. “It’s just an absolute nightmare down there. It’s the only word I can use to describe it.”Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers were affected and that it had cancelled more than 50 scheduled flights.EasyJet said some of its flights were “unable to operate” and that the system failure caused “delays to flights across Europe.”Other affected airports included London Stansted and London City, as well as airports in Manchester, Birmingham and Scotland. Passengers have been advised to check their flight status with their airline before travelling.

items.title: Pakistan issues warning after attack on Saudi
items.summary: Islamabad: Pakistan said there should be "no ambiguity" that an attack on any one of the three members of the newly formed Makkah Defence Alliance would be treated as an attack on all, as he warned that the pact could become operative following Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia.Defence Minister Khawaja Asif's remarks on Tuesday come hours after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched a wave of missile and drone attacks on Saudi Arabia, targeting cities and economic and energy infrastructure and injuring at least 73 civilians.The minister said any unprovoked aggression against a member state, or a spillover of the Yemen conflict into Saudi Arabia, would activate the collective-defence provisions of the agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in Makkah last month."There should be no ambiguity; there is no need for any clarity that this is a joint defence agreement," Asif said in an interview with Geo TV channel. Pakistan would honour its commitments to Saudi Arabia under the pact, he said."There should be no doubt about this. We are bound by the terms and conditions of this pact and, God willing, we will honour them in case there is a need," Asif asserted.Asif, however, said he was not aware of any contact between Pakistan and Saudi Arabia following the Houthi attacks.He stressed that the agreement was defensive in nature and did not authorise the three countries to launch attacks against another state on their own initiative."This is not an aggressive agreement under which the three countries would, on their own initiative, attack another country. But if there is any aggression against one member state, all three member states will respond," the minister said.He expressed hope that tensions would subside, but warned the Houthis against extending the Yemen conflict beyond the country's borders."If they try to export them, the clauses of this agreement to counter aggression will become operative," Asif reiterated.Asif described the Houthis as "non-state actors" and said there was sympathy for Iran across the Muslim world, including Yemen, over its ongoing conflict with the United States.He, however, cautioned against allowing such sentiments to be used to widen an existing bilateral dispute.The minister said the Makkah alliance could serve as a deterrent and did not necessarily mean that the three countries would respond to aggression with military force."We don't need to respond to a brick with a stone," he said, arguing that the combined military capabilities of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye should themselves act as a deterrent.He said Saudi Arabia should not be dragged into what he described as an internal conflict in Yemen and expressed hope that diplomatic efforts could help prevent further escalation.A Saudi-led coalition of Arab states has backed Yemen's internationally recognised government in its war against the Houthis for more than a decade.The Houthis said Tuesday's attacks were retaliation for dozens of recent Saudi airstrikes on areas of northwestern Yemen under their control. On Monday, the group accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in the city of Al Hazm, killing at least 11 people.

items.title: Delhi PG residents ask: Are we safe?
items.summary: New Delhi: For students and young professionals who leave their hometowns for Delhi in pursuit of their dreams, a paying guest accommodation gradually becomes much more than four walls and a bed. It becomes a second home where they return after college or work, have their meals, prepare for exams, attend late-night meetings and call their families before going to sleep.But the collapse of a five-storey building housing a boys' PG in south Delhi's Satya Niketan on September 6, which claimed seven lives, has shaken that sense of security and made many question whether the place they call home is truly safe.Also Read: Satya Niketan tragedy: Supreme Court may examine building safety, construction violations across IndiaFor students and young professionals currently living in PGs across Delhi-NCR, the tragedy has brought a question into their rooms that many had never considered before: Do I really know how safe the building I sleep in is?Until now, choosing a PG was largely about rent, food, Wi-Fi and proximity to college or the workplace. The condition of the building, its permissions and approvals, or what would happen in an emergency often remained outside that calculation.Sneha Mishra, who lives at 'New PG for Girls' in Sant Nagar, said the collapse has changed the way she looks at the place she has come to regard as home after moving to Delhi from Deoghar, Jharkhand."When I came to Delhi from Deoghar, this PG became my second home. I eat, study and sleep here, but I never really thought about whether the place I call home is actually safe," Mishra told ANI.That thought, she said, now follows her even when she is trying to sleep."Earlier, I never thought about the condition of the building. Now, when I go to sleep, there is a question in my mind - what if the building we trust with our lives is not safe?" she told ANI.The worry does not stop with the young people living inside these buildings. It travels back home, to parents who send their children to Delhi believing they have found a secure place to live."Our parents send us here believing we are safe. After Satya Niketan, many of us have started looking at the roof over our heads differently," Mishra told ANI.But for many young people, finding a safer place is not simply a matter of making a choice. It is also a matter of being able to afford one. A better-maintained PG can mean a higher monthly rent, something that can be difficult for a student or someone earning an entry-level salary. In a city where every extra thousand rupees matters, safety can end up competing with affordability.Shilpashree Mondal, who lives in a PG in Noida, stated that her budget leaves little room for choice.Also Read: Buried aspirations: Grieving families say, if this isn’t murder, what is? after losing CA and IAS aspirants to Satya Niketan PG disaster"I don't think even a working woman like me has much of a real choice when it comes to choosing where to live. Budget decides most of it, especially in a city like Delhi, where finding a safe and affordable place can be difficult," Mondal told ANI.The Satya Niketan collapse initially frightened Mondal. But soon, the fear turned into a closer look at the place where she herself lives."I started thinking, what if something like this happens to my PG too? I somehow convinced myself that it wouldn't happen, but there are already things that worry me, like problems with the water supply, poor hygiene and dampness in the walls," she said.Often, she said, the reality of a PG becomes clear only after moving in."The owner and caretakers often make things look safer and better than they actually are, but you only realise the real problems once you start living there," Mondal told ANI.For Pallavi Joshi, who hails from Uttarakhand's Haldwand has been living in a Delhi PG for nearly two years, the collapse has changed an otherwise ordinary nightly routine."I had never thought about the structure of my PG before. After Satya Niketan, I started noticing how my building is designed and wondering whether there are enough safety measures. Even at night, I sometimes think about what would happen if something went wrong here," Joshi told ANI.Joshi told ANI that neither her PG owner nor anyone from the management approached the occupants after the incident to discuss their concerns or assure them about the safety of the building.She said PG owners often focus on receiving rent on time, while concerns over safety, hygiene and what happens during an emergency receive less attention.For Vijaya Roy, a student of Delhi University's Ramanujan College preparing for the CAT examination, the uncertainty begins with something as basic as knowing whether the place has the necessary permissions.Around 20 to 25 people live in her PG, she told ANI, but occupants are not always told whether the property has the required approvals."We don't even know whether they have permission from the Municipal Corporation of Delhi or not. When we first come to the PG, they demand documents from us, but they don't show any papers to us," Roy told ANI.For Roy, students should not have to take the owner's word for it when it comes to the building they are going to sleep in every night."It should be made mandatory that tenants are able to get the papers from PG owners, so that they know whether the building has the proper permissions and whether the regulations are being followed," she said.For Delhi University students, the shortage of affordable hostel accommodation makes that dependence on PGs even greater, Roy said."If adequate hostel facilities are available in colleges, students will have another option. PG owners will not have the same monopoly and may be forced to improve conditions," she told ANI.For these students and young professionals, the Satya Niketan collapse is no longer something they simply watched on a news screen. It has changed the way they look at their own rooms at the damp patch on a wall, the makeshift partition, the crowded staircase or the roof above their bed.Keping student safety as a priority, the Delhi government is working on a comprehensive policy to regulate paying guest (PG) accommodations in the national capital, with Urban Development Minister Ashish Sood outlining a series of proposed measures aimed at strengthening safety, security and rent regulation for students.Under the proposed policy, PG operators would be required to obtain a PG Operating Licence and complete both police and municipal verification before running their establishments. The proposed rules would also make CCTV cameras mandatory at entrances and in common areas of PG accommodations, with recordings required to be preserved for 30 days.For PGs housing 15 or more students, operators would be required to employ a licensed night guard between 10 pm and 6 am. Visitor registers would also be made mandatory, while non-resident visitors would be permitted entry between 8 am and 9 pm.The policy would further require every PG to have a warden either residing at the premises or maintaining an office within a 500-metre radius. The warden would have to be physically available within 15 minutes in case of an emergency. To address concerns over arbitrary and high rents, the proposed policy envisages a Rent Regulation Committee that would determine rent bands for different areas.The rent bands would take into account factors including occupancy levels, amenities provided, prevailing market rates and the proximity of the PG to colleges and public transport. The draft framework also proposes the creation of an Institutional Accommodation Committee, comprising college officials, student representatives, a municipal representative and a police liaison officer.

items.summary:
The United States is banning dairy products, most alcoholic beverages and motorcycles from Canada, the White House said on Tuesday, as the trade war between the two nations escalates.
The ban will take effect in three weeks and comes after Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs on USD 20 billion in US imports earlier Tuesday.
US President Donald Trump on Tuesday moved to shut Canadian products out of large, long-term US government contracts as Canada's retaliatory tariffs took effect and Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed to speed efforts to reduce the country's dependence on the United States.
Trump directed the US General Services Administration to declare Canadian products ineligible for those contracts until Canada allows "full and fair reciprocity" for American products.
Earlier on Tuesday, Carney said Canada's strategy was about becoming more independent. "It's about ensuring that no country can hold us hostage. And that we can live how we want to live."

Over 1,000 flights cancelled in Britain due to air traffic control issue
items.summary:
An air traffic control problem disrupted travel across Britain on Tuesday, cancelling more than 1,000 flights and leaving passengers stranded for hours on airport runways and in terminals, according to flight-tracking website Flightradar24.
Britain's National Air Traffic Services said it had resolved a problem in its flight processing system in the evening but delays rippled across 15 UK airports and beyond as airlines and airports worked to clear a huge backlog of delayed flights.
Josie Donoghue spent three hours stuck on a plane at Gatwick before her Ryanair flight to Ireland was cancelled.
"Getting through that airport was like trying to get out of Alcatraz," she said, referring to the notorious former island prison in San Francisco Bay. "It's just an absolute nightmare down there. It's the only word I can use to describe it."

US destroys 5 Iranian oil tankers after missile attacks on Navy warship
items.summary:
The US military has destroyed five Iranian crude oil tankers following attacks on a US warship by Iran's Revolutionary Guard, US Central Command said in a social media post on Tuesday.
The US strikes were in response to two Iranian efforts to hit the warship with ballistic missiles over the past two days, the statement added.
Iranian state television also reported the strikes, saying US forces attacked at least three Iranian oil tankers near the southern port of Jask and near Kharg Island in the Persian Gulf. It said the crews were evacuated.
The latest tit-for-tat strikes come as Washington and Tehran lurch back toward fighting during more than six months of war.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US will not allow Iran's attacks to go unanswered.
"Iran continues to try to hit US naval ships. And for every time they do that or try to do that, they're going to lose tankers. And I think you'll see that again today," Rubio told reporters on Tuesday when asked about the latest .

items.title: Meta launches personal AI agent 'Muse' to help with everyday tasks
items.summary:
Meta launched on Tuesday a personal artificial intelligence agent, Muse, for people 18 and over who are looking for help with day-to-day tasks like schedules, shopping and, in the company's words, turning "long-term goals into action plans."
The parent company of Instagram and Facebook is stressing the safety and privacy features of the agent, which for now is only available in the US Muse, Meta said, runs on a dedicated, secure virtual machine that houses both the agent and the user's data.
People can message the agent in a separate app, called Muse, or message it in WhatsApp. It can handle simple tasks like sending an email or booking travel, or bigger, long-term goals like creating a yearlong exercise plan or setting up a new business.
"Once a person shares a goal with Muse, it helps them develop a personalised plan and coordinate their time and resources, then advances the work on its own. It can open a browser, fill out forms, and negotiate on their behalf," Meta said in a blog

items.title: MCD begins demolition of building beside collapsed Satya Niketan structure
items.summary:
The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) on Tuesday began the controlled demolition of a building adjoining the structure that collapsed in south Delhi's Satya Niketan on September 6, officials said.
An MCD official said the building had been declared dangerous.
"We started demolition of the adjoining building today, and the work was stopped in the evening. The demolition exercise will resume tomorrow morning," the official said.
The building housed a girls' paying guest accommodation and was evacuated after the collapse of the neighbouring five-storey structure, which left at least seven people dead and five injured on Sunday.
The same day, the MCD issued an order for property no 13 in Satya Niketan, directing the owner or occupier to tear down the structure, citing it as a threat to residents and neighbouring buildings.
MCD officials had earlier said that the students had already vacated the building and were returning only to collect their belongings before the demolition.

UK sanctions 'illegal' Israeli settlements in West Bank, bans imports
items.summary:
The UK on Tuesday announced sanctions on Israeli settlements in the West Bank, banning the import of goods from the occupied Palestinian territories which it declared as "illegal".
UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband was joined by Prime Minister Andy Burnham in the House of Commons as he delivered a statement to condemn the "ethnic cleansing of Palestinians" in West Bank settlements.
While highlighting his own "proud British Jew" heritage, Miliband announced a "new comprehensive sanctions regime with appropriate religious exemptions".
"The government believes the unlawfulness of the occupation should be reflected in the economic relationships we choose to have with the occupied territories," Miliband told MPs.
"So I can announce today that we will introduce an import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories," he said.
Miliband said action would be taken against specific companies and individuals providing construction, infrastructure, financing or real estate
